full_judgment:
This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 4.6.86 passed by the Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka convicting the appellant for violating the labour law in not implementing the judgment in the original case in full as passed by the First Labour Court, Dhaka, directing the appellants to pay the complainant Tk. 3,972/72, in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month each. 

 2. Facts leading to this case are that respondent No. 1 namely, Sheikh Shahabuddin, an employee under the Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation filed, a Complaint case being No. 295 of 1982 against appellant No. 1 before the First Labour Court, Dhaka alleging that for trade union activities he has been removed from his service illegally and without lawful authority with a prayer for re-instatement in his service or alternatively to direct the second party to pay termination dues amounting to a sum of Tk. 5,740.20 as in the break up of the plaint still remaining paid by the corporation. The Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation contested the case by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint stating further that the termination of the respondent was simpliciter and not for any trade union activities or for any misconduct and that he has been paid in full all the termination benefits. The learned Labour Court on an examination of records and after hearing the parties by its judgment dated 1.6.85 disposed of the matter with the following order: 

 3. Respondent No. 1 thereafter applied to the Corporation for reinstatment as per judgment and he was replied to by the Corporation and was informed by the Corporation that his prayer could not be entertained by the Corporation for re-instatement and as the alternative order for payment of termination benefit is accepted by the B.R.T.C. and as he was al-ready paid the termination benefit in full and as only an amount of Tk. 45.02 was due to him he was asked to accept the same through cheque No. 723198 but the respondent did not accept that but filed a Criminal Case being No. 74 of 1985 before the First Labour Court for non-implementation of the judgment of the Labour Court passed in Complaint Case No. 295 of 1982. The Criminal Case No. 74 of 1985 was also contested by the Corporation and it was submitted before the learned Labour Court by the Corporation that the said Criminal Case was totally misconceived and misconstrued as the respondent has been paid the termination benefit in full and he has in fact no cause of action. The Labour Court, however, came to a finding that the complainant had not been paid the compensation money in full as allowed under the Labour Law vide section 19 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act an thereby had violated the law by not implementing the judgment in the original case in full and the complaint case was allowed in part on contest without costs against which this appeal was preferred which is heard and disposed of by this judgment. 

 4. Mr. Md. Aminul Haque, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, submitted that the judgment and order passed by the Labour Court is not a proper judgment because the Labour Court failed to take into consideration in spite of the documents placed before the court showing that the payment of termination benefit was in full and in accordance with law. He futher submitted that the Labour Court failed to take into consideration that in the break up of the original complaint case even the complainant did not ask for any compensation due to him under section 19 of the Standing Orders Act but prayed for gratuity and that was legally done by the complainant because under the Rules framed by the Corporation, the Corporation is to pay gratuity in case of termination 10 days in a year on the basis of basic pay and have calculated the same, according to the Corporation, on his basic salary which was Tk. 468/-. That was also the case of the complainant in his plaint petition, where he submitted his basic salary to be Tk. 468/-in paragraph 1 of the complaint. Gratuity at the rate of Tk. 468/- for 30 days in a year for 14 years, comes to Tk. 6,463.80 and it was offered to the complainant and he accepted the same though under protest. In his complaint case he calculated the amount to be Tk. 10,836.00 for 420 days wages at the rate of Tk. 875/-per month which would cover allowances at the rate of 7k. 140/-, House rent Tk. 163.00, Ration Allowance Tk. 25.00 per month, Medical allowance Tk. 60.00 per month which is not a part of his basic pay. This is essentially a wrong calcation which is apparent on the face of the record ar. A is submitted. by the learned Advocates that the labour Court did not at all consider this aspect of the matter and came to a finding of non-implementation of judgment when there was no specific order of payment of any specific sum as termination benefit to the employee and in the absence of such specific order there cannot be any violation or non-implementation of the judgment of the Labour Court and the Labour Court erred in law in coming to a finding of non-implementation by a wrong calculation of his own and that also under section 26 of the Employment of Labour Standing Order Act. This was done by the Labour Court without jurisdiction and therefore need be set aside. In sup-port of his contention the learned Counsel has referred to a decision, reported in 41 DLR at page 203, to which I shall advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. 

 5. The learned Advocate Mr. Aminul Huq, for the respondent, on the other hand, submitted that the complainant was entitled to compensation benefit in case of termination simpliciter under the proviso to section 19 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act and only because he has not asked for it in the break up of the complaint petition it cannot be said that he was not entitled to it and in the instant case it is apparent that this 30 days in a year compensation had not been paid by the Corporation to the complainant because it has been stated by the Corporation, in their calculation sheet, that as to this amount he is not entitled under the Rules framed by the corporation. According to the learned Advocate, there lies the non-implementation of the judgment. He was not paid in full the compensation benefit which he was allowed under the Labour Law. 

 6. In the instant case, from a reading of the judgment as passed by the Labour Court in the original complaint case No. 295 of 1982 it is seen that in the said judgment delivered by the Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka, which states that the learned members have been consulted in the matter, came to a finding that it is not clear from papers filed as to whether the petitioner was paid his termination benefit in full and if the second party has paid less, balance, if any, should be paid to him. This is of course a matter of record. After finding this the court orders that the second party be directed to pay the first party the balance of the termination money, if any, after consulting all papers relevant or in the alternative the second party may re-instate the petitioner in his former job after adjustment of all amounts paid to him. From a reading of the said judgment it is thus seen that the Labour Court could not come to a definite finding as to whether the petitioner has been paid in full or paid less and left it for the corporation to re-examine the matter and to pay the full termination benefit if he was paid less or to re-instate. 

 7. There was, therefore, no direction for payment of any specific sum as termination benefit due to the complainant and it is thus not understood where there was the violation or non-implementation of any specific order passed by the Court. Further, it is seen that in the Criminal Case filed before the Labour Court by the complainant it was not the specific case or his case at all that he was not paid the termination money as allowed under section 19 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act but rather it was his case that though the appellant No. 1 agreed to re-instate him he was asked to take termination benefit which was the alternative given in the judgment. It is seen that the Labour Court on the basis of this allegation, alleged in the criminal case filed under section 26 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, came to a finding, going beyond the pleading of the parties, that there was a non-payment of compensation to an amount of Tk. 3,972.28 which was due to him under law and as a result the accused person had violated the law by not implementing the judgment in full. 

 8. This was done by the court in exercise of the powers under section 26 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act for non-complying with the order passed by the Court under section 25 of the said .Act, which appears to be an exercise of power travelling beyond the power. Under section 26 of the Act, for a court to come to a finding that there was a non-compliance with the Court's order, must out of necessity strictly limit itself within the order passed specifically by the court and not by any inference or analogical deduction drawn from it. In the instant case from the original judgment and order passed by the Labour Court which has been referred to earlier, it has been found that the Labour Court itself did not come to a finding that there was a full payment of termination benefit or less payment of termination benefit and directed the second party namely, the Corporation who is the appellant before this court and who have been convicted subsequently to examine the matter and if paid less to pay the complainant in full and it is seen that in their written objection to the criminal case they have categorically stated that vide Ext. A that he was paid gratuity at the rate of his basic pay being Tk. 468/-per month for 420 days, plus 30 days earned leave, 90 days notice pay, D.A. increased pay and deducted his loan of Tk. 464/- and travelling paid in advance which altogether comes to Tk.738/- and after deducting that amount from the total dues of Tk. 9957.90—Tk. 738.00, he was paid in full Tk.9218.90 which he however accepted with protest and that the amount of compensation money which he claims is not due to him because under the provision of Rules as framed by the corporation he was to be paid gratuity 30 days per year of the basic pay in lieu of compensation of 30 days basic pay as under section 19 of the Act and the petitioner was aware of it and therefore in his complaint petition he never claimed any amount under section 19. 

 10. A somewhat similar matter came up for decision before a Division Bench of this Court in Writ jurisdiction, in the case of Sekander Miah Vs. Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka reported in 41 DLR Dhaka page 203. In that case under report the respondent challenged his dismissal from service being illegal and malafide. The Labour Court allowed the case on contest in part. The order of dismissal from service was set aside but his service was terminated in accordance with law in terms of section 19 of the Standing Orders Act and it was ordered that the respondent corporation shall give all benefit under the said provision of law and the second party was directed to give effect to that order within 60 days. As per terms of this judgment and order, respondent No. 2 was paid termination benefit of an amount of Tk. 26,100.33 but he made out a case that he was entitled to a total sum of Tk. 84,483.00 and having been paid only Tk. 26,100.33 he claimed a further sum of Tk. 58,382.67 which having not been paid he filed a Criminal case against the corporation under section 26 of the Standing Orders Act. The Labour Court found that as the claim of the respondent went unchallenged at the trial, he was entitled to the same and finding so, convicted the petitioners for commit-ting an offence under section 26 of the Act. They were directed to pay the aforesaid sum within 45 days, which was challenged before the Division Bench of this Court and the Court in making the Rule absolute found that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under section 26 is not attracted unless the accused refused to comply with die order passed by the Labour Court under section 25 of the Act and the Labour Court in the instant case having merely declared that the respondent was to get all benefit un-der section 19 of the Act and having not specifically mentioned any quantum of termination benefit, the accused could not be said to have refused or failed to comply with the order passed by the Court under section 25 and the court found that for any balance of Payment of Wages under the payment of wages Act and under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance any worker may apply to the Labour Court for the enforcement of any right guaranteed or secured to him under any law and as such the respondent should apply to the Labour Court under section 34 of the Industrial. Relations Ordinance for determination of the quantum of termination benefit and the court further held that after Labour. Court passed a general or-der as to termination benefit of the work-men, the Labour Court has no jurisdiction to determine the quantum under section 26 of the said Act and Labour Court can punish an offender only for refusal or failure to comply with an order and not refusal or failure to comply with an indefinite order. 

 11. I am in respectful agreement with the finding as above which is also in complete accord with the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect, that if a person is to be found guilty for non-implementation of any order, the order must be specific and whether an order has been followed, non  implemented or not must be decided by reference to  the order itself, to be specified in it and not by any inference or analogical deduction drawn from imaginary or speculative facts not disclosed, and further, in the instant case a judgment travelling beyond the pleading of the parties would be bad in law as that would be an exercise of power travelling beyond the plaint in deciding a dispute and an issue not pending before the Court, directly or even incidentally. In the instant case the complainant workmen who is not in service of the Corporation, if aggrieved yet, may have the quantum of termination benefit fixed or determined by due process of law, may be by filing an application under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance if so advised; but it is not for the Labour Court to decide the said quantum under section 26 of the Standing Order Act which it could do under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act while delivering the original judgment.
